newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: New Argentine customs head sees "scandalous" fraud.
newsitem.headline: New Argentine customs head sees "scandalous" fraud.

text.p: The new head of Argentina's customs service, appointed as part of a corruption crackdown, described the level of fraud there on Wednesday as "surprising and scandalous."
Carlos Silvani, director of the taxation bureau, was given responsibility for the customs branch under a merger of the offices announced by President Carlos Menem on Tuesday night.
Silvani, asked by Radio Del Plata on Wednesday about the extent of corruption in customs, said, "I think it is surprising, it is scandalous."

Menem, in a televised address to the nation late on Tuesday, announced the customs office would come under close scrutiny to help destroy mafia-like organisations that were cheating the state of billions of dollars a year.
"I ask all Argentines to continue supporting us in this authentic crusade to combat corruption," Menem said.
The government believes corrupt customs officials have set up a "parallel" customs service to smuggle in goods worth $10 billion -- costing the state $3 billion in lost duties.
Silvani said he suspected corrupt officials were finding ways to fool the custom's new sophisticated computing system.
"I don't think the system created these irregularities but rather there was only partial or incomplete application of the system, which allowed this type of fraud," Silvani said.

Police have raided customs offices, supermarkets and banks in recent days, seizing goods and documents. Seven people were arrested in one case, including one customs official and six customs "fixers", and 10 others are hiding from police.
Penal court judge Julio Cruciani ordered five people arrested on Wednesday in a separate customs probe.

Officials say that typically, corrupt customs employees help others evade duties by marking Argentine-bound containers as being in transit to other countries and sending them to warehouses where the goods are removed for local sale.
The government estimates overall yearly tax evasion at about $20 billion, half the size of state spending.
Several former customs chiefs are on trial for corruption. Judge Cruciani on Wednesday likened the appointment of officials to that post to a sentence to the electric chair.
